own_scenes.place: El Sur, Watts, Newark, Detroit y Oakland
own_scenes.desc: «No se puede hablar del funk sin hablar de la Revolución Negra» (Shock G). Las sentadas, los Freedom Rides y la Marcha sobre Washington de 1963 llevaron el gospel a la calle («A Change Is Gonna Come», «Keep on Pushing»), pero pese a las leyes la masa negra apenas notó cambios. Malcolm X habló por los desposeídos y su asesinato en 1965 dejó un vacío: «It was a funky deal» (Etheridge Knight). Vinieron Watts (con el DJ Magnificent Montague pinchando «Burn, Baby, Burn»), el grito de «Black Power» en la marcha de Meredith de 1966, el SNCC sin blancos, los Panteras Negras de Huey Newton y Bobby Seale en Oakland (armados en el Capitolio de California en 1967, «la mayor amenaza» para Hoover), Newark y Detroit en 1967, los disturbios tras el asesinato de King en 1968, los puños de Tommie Smith y John Carlos en México y el «ningún Vietcong me llamó nigger» de Muhammad Ali. Futuros músicos funk (Marshall Jones de los Ohio Players, Bootsy en Cincinnati, Mudbone Cooper en Baltimore) tiraron piedras en los disturbios: la universidad de la calle. «Say It Loud – I’m Black and I’m Proud» de James Brown convirtió «black» en elogio; «Black Is Beautiful» invirtió siglos de lenguaje y hasta «funky» se reivindicó. Esa libertad de redefinir lo negro fue la incubadora del funk.

refs.q: Things became very funky indeed after the focal point of Malcolm X was no longer there.
refs.para: Things became very funky indeed after the focal point of Malcolm X was no longer there. It appeared that the movement was heading toward a more intense, nitty-gritty level. It was getting funky out there. At the time of the assassination of Malcolm X in February 1965, the black American population had a number of nonviolent organizational resources to fight racism and advocate for resources, such as the Congress of Racial Equality (CORE), the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC), and Dr. King’s organization, the Southern Christian Leadership Conference. But the death of Malcolm signified a dramatic new direction in the movement. For many young blacks, the hypocrisy of nonviolence in the face of a violent system was affirmed by Malcolm’s murder. The presumption of tolerance was wearing thin on an entire generation. Later that year, in August, the first of many large-scale riots to sweep the nation throughout the remainder of the decade hit Los Angeles and lasted for three weeks, burning block after block and killing thirty-nine people. (The Los Angeles radio deejay Magnificent Montague stirred up the controversy by playing the pop tune “Burn, Baby Burn” by the Creators regularly as the city was consumed.) The Watts Riots were a tragedy to some and a battle call to others, but nobody thought they would be the last. The requisite shock and outrage were heard, a federal commission was appointed to “study” the causes of the riot, and the pressure mounted. Ultimately, rebellion became the method of choice for protest across black America.

refs.q: The “Black Panther Party for Self-Defense” was founded in Oakland, California, in 1966
refs.para: The “Black Panther Party for Self-Defense” was founded in Oakland, California, in 1966 by Merritt College students Huey P. Newton and Bobby Seale. Their plans involved community policing, active community centers with health and education services, and a far-reaching plan for black liberation that included an inevitable revolution led by black Americans. After months of following the police, reading the penal code out loud to arresting officers, and developing a small following in the Oakland area, the group took their case to the nation. In full view of the national media, the Panthers walked into the California State Legislature in 1967 wearing dark leather jackets and dark shades, and, armed with rifles, demanding an audience. refs.q: The same environment that created funk created the Black Panthers to start with.
refs.para: The legacy of the Black Panthers can be seen on the cover of Funkadelic’s 1979 Uncle Jam Wants You album, designed in the same format as the famous Black Panther publicity poster of Huey P. Newton—with George Clinton as Uncle Jam in Newton’s place. Rap producer Claude “Paradise” Gray of X-Clan put the Panthers in perspective: “The same environment that created funk created the Black Panthers to start with. The Black Panthers were created out of the same idea. It was a rebellion.”

refs.q: It was the essence of the Black Revolution, it was the incubator of The Funk
refs.para: The affirmation that black is actually beautiful was as total as a transformation could be. It was the essence of the Black Revolution, it was the incubator of The Funk, and it was the inspiration for the overall social revolution of the 1960s.

own_scenes.place: Lowndes County (Alabama), Greenwood (Misisipi), Chicago y Detroit
own_scenes.desc: En Lowndes County, Stokely Carmichael y el SNCC crearon una organización de votantes con una pantera negra como símbolo frente al gallo blanco de los demócratas de Wallace, y ya llevaban armas. El SNCC condenó Vietnam en enero de 1966 y eligió a Carmichael presidente en mayo. El 16 de junio, tras su vigesimoséptima detención en plena Marcha contra el Miedo, gritó en Greenwood «What do you want? BLACK POWER!»: autodeterminación, no violencia, pero la prensa lo convirtió en amenaza. La espiral se aceleró: gases en Canton, disturbios en el West Side de Chicago (julio), Watts «aún hirviendo». En la marcha, un joven improvisaba «Freedom got a shotgun» y la multitud contestaba con el «na na-ne-na-na» de «Land of 1000 Dances». El 30 de julio, el día que Carmichael hablaba en Detroit, el disco de Pickett entraba en el Billboard.

influences.name: Derechos civiles: de Selma a la Marcha contra el Miedo

refs.q: The move towards self-determination was already moving into a new phase. It was all coalescing around two words: ‘Black Power’.
refs.para: The move towards self-determination was already moving into a new phase. It was all coalescing around two words: ‘Black Power’. The phrase was not new – the famed author Richard Wright had written a book with that title back in 1954 – but it was definitely in the air. In their 16 June issue Jet featured a report about SNCC policy in Lowndes County entitled ‘Carmichael’s Stand on Mobilising Black Power Is Unequivocal’.
refs.chapter: Julio: Land of 1000 Dances: Tamla, el soul y la Marcha contra el Miedo

refs.q: Black Power was an honest attempt to push black politics forward, but it became trapped within an accelerating spiral
refs.para: Black Power was an honest attempt to push black politics forward, but it became trapped within an accelerating spiral: the violence directed by whites against blacks caused anger and frustration; this anger and frustration resulted in the abandonment of non-violence as a policy; the abandonment of non-violence opened up the gates to black violence, which then created more reactive white violence, which created more anger and frustration … and so on.
